Question: As a soldier, have you ever accidentally killed an innocent civilian?
Old_Answer: Two peasants drove with their tractor over an anti-tank mine which I had placed there earlier. This happened in Kosovo during the time of the NATO airstrikes. There was a lot of fighting on the ground, especially in our area, but to my surprise, there were still some civilians around. We suspected that at least some of these folks were Serbian spies, but we couldn’t prove it. After an enemy offensive, my guerrilla unit had to withdraw to the mountains. Before we left, we mined all the approach routes the enemy could use. Whenever we encountered a farmer, we informed them about the mines so they could avoid getting hurt. Three days later, after the enemy offensive had ended, we returned to “our” valley” to remove the mines. Some of our devices had killed enemy soldiers, while others were duds, but when I arrived at a small road crossing where we had placed two anti-tank mines, I found an overturned and badly damaged tractor. In Kosovo, during the time of this incident. While looking for the second mine (the first one had been activated by the tractor), a peasant from a nearby village approached us and told us that two of his neighbors had been killed when their tractor drove over the mine. He pointed to a spot nearby where I could see a shoe covered in blood. We didn't tell him who had planted the mines. I didn't see any point in doing so. These people came from a village that (to my best knowledge) had never supported the guerrilla. And the fact that this guy had been around while our enemy was in the area made him double suspicious. I never thought twice about this incident, and I never felt bad about it. In war, sh*t happens.

Old_Answer: This issue is a bit more complicated. Ukraine acknowledges that is does not have enough troops (especially infantry); however, this is not because the recruiting pool has dried up. There are still between two and three and a half million able-bodied men inside Ukraine and another 600k in Western Europe. Ukraine could theoretically draft, train, and equip most of them but this would a.) cost a lot of money and b) completely ruin the economy. To get a recruit frontline ready costs about 20,000 dollars and this money has to come from somewhere. The main reason the Russians have fewer manpower problems than Ukraine is only partly due to their bigger population size: First of all, Russia doesn't care about the quality of the people they mobilize. Hard-core criminals, drug addicts, and mentally challenged people are always welcome to join. Of course, this makes for more recruits (without having to pull people away from their workplace and damaging the economy) but not for better ones. At the same time, the costs to train and mobilize these new “mobniks” are only a fraction of what Ukraine is paying. Again, lower costs mean you can recruit more people with less money. In addition, Russia often doesn't pay their soldiers’ salaries, doesn't take care of the wounded, and lets the dead ones rot on the battlefield (to avoid having to pay compensation to their families).
